about: Hamwic (Southampton, the St Mary's shore), the West Saxons' trading town on the Itchen, 793 to 1066. Written 6 Oct 2026 from Design/content/dossiers/hamwic.md and the spine; a draft for the user to overwrite. Invented people are marked historical false; (?) marks what could not be checked. Woven with the other ports of the region on 7 Oct 2026: ties answered both ways (the ale-wives, the riddlers, the pilots), beats added at Lundenwic, Sarre, Fordwic, Dofras, Gipeswic and Dommoc, and the region's cards (Data/encounters/england_south_east_793.json) hung on the sites and the beats.

ports.summary: Hamwic is the West Saxons' one great trading town: an open, timber-built place of gravel streets on the west bank of the Itchen, with no wall, no tower and no quay, where ships are drawn up on a shelving beach. In 793 King Beorhtric's reeve keeps it, and the coin in hand is King Offa's. A merchant comes for wool and English cloth, and brings wine, black Seine pots, glass and quernstones; Rouen is a day and a night away with the wind on the beam.
ports.seasons: The wool comes in after the June shearing (?) and the Frankish ships come for it through the summer; pilgrims take ship at summer's end, and the wool men cross for the fair of Saint-Denis in October. The tide here comes twice: high water stands for hours and the ebb is short and hard, so a boat can beach or float off at almost any hour but must not be caught on the mud flats when the water goes.

history.text: Abbot Cyneberht, whose minster lay near this water, baptised two princes of Wight before King Caedwalla had them killed. Bede calls this shore Jutish.
history.source: Bede, Ecclesiastical History IV.16; dossier hamwic [B; M]

history.text: Oak was felled soon after this year for the first works of the town, probably under King Ine. Its straight gravel streets were laid before the houses.
history.source: A. D. Morton, Excavations at Hamwic 1 (CBA Research Report 84, 1992), pp. 1-77

history.text: About this year Willibald and his father and brother took ship for the Seine near 'the mart called Hamwic', paid their fares to the master, and pitched their tents by the river at Rouen.
history.source: Huneberc, Hodoeporicon of Willibald; Morton 1992. The year is about 721 (?)

history.text: 'Homwic' is listed among the towns burnt this year. No burnt layer has been found in the ground.
history.source: Morton 1992 (the annal in Symeon of Durham's Historia regum (?))

history.text: An oak was felled near Hamwic and went into an English clinker ship. Her planks ended their days on Walcheren.
history.source: Ufkes 2012, Paleo-aktueel 23; Design/content/dossiers/walichrum.md

history.text: Beorhtric took the kingdom of the West Saxons. In 789 he took to wife Eadburh, King Offa's daughter; and in his days three ships of Northmen came to Portland, and the reeve Beaduheard, who took them for traders, was killed.
history.source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 784, 787 (Ingram 1823); en.wikipedia Beorhtric of Wessex, Beaduheard

history.text: King Beorhtric died and Ecgberht came home from the land of the Franks and took the kingdom.
history.source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 800 (Ingram 1823); chronicle_793.json

history.text: On the day after Christmas King Ecgberht was at 'Omtune' and gave land by his charter.
history.source: Sawyer 273: https://esawyer.lib.cam.ac.uk/charter/273.html

history.text: Ealdorman Wulfheard fought at Hamtun against thirty-three ship-crews, made great slaughter and had the victory; and he died the same year. King Aethelwulf gave land to his thegn Duda 'in the royal vill called Hamtun'. About now the West Saxon mint stopped.
history.source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 837 (Ingram 1823); Sawyer 288; M. Dolley, Proc. Hampshire Field Club 27 (1970)

history.text: Northmen sacked Quentovic, crossed the sea and plundered 'Hamwig and Nordhunnwig'. The Chronicle says nothing of it, and it may be the fight of 840 told twice (?).
history.source: Nithard, Histories IV.3; Morton 1992

history.text: About this year the town on the Itchen stood largely empty. Silver was put in the ground about 850 and again about 870, and not fetched.
history.source: Morton 1992; Hodges 1981 ends the town about 840, Addyman and Hill 1968 about 940-970

history.text: A great fleet came up and stormed Winchester. Ealdorman Osric with the men of Hamtunscir, and Ealdorman Aethelwulf with the men of Berkshire, fought it and put it to flight.
history.source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 860 (Ingram 1823)

history.text: From about this year a new ditched town of some six hectares rose to the south-west, on the Test shore; the Burghal Hidage rates Hamtun at 150 hides. It throve after 950.
history.source: Morton 1992; en.wikipedia Burghal Hidage (written c. 880-920)

history.text: About this year King Aethelstan's law allowed two moneyers at Hamtun, and forbade any man to buy goods worth more than twenty pence outside a port.
history.source: II Aethelstan 12, 14 (the law itself not opened (?)); chronicle_793.json; Design/content/economy/silver_coin.md

history.text: 'Southampton was plundered by a pirate-army, and most of the population slain or imprisoned.'
history.source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 980, tr. J. Ingram 1823: https://avalon.law.yale.edu/medieval/ang10.asp

history.text: Olaf and Swein came to London with ninety-four ships and were beaten off. They took winter quarters at Southampton and were fed from all the West Saxon land, and were paid sixteen thousand pounds. Bishop Aelfheah and Ealdorman Aethelweard fetched Olaf to the king at Andover, where he promised never to come back in enmity.
history.source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 994 (Ingram 1823); Florence of Worcester (Forester 1854)

history.text: The bishops, abbots and ealdormen came to Cnut at Southampton, forswore the line of Aethelred and swore to him. London chose Edmund.
history.source: Florence of Worcester 1016 (Forester 1854)

history.text: About this year the mint at Hamtun closed for good. Its pennies from about 973 had been signed both HAMTUN and HAMWIC.
history.source: Addyman and Hill 1968, with M. Dolley on the coins; A. R. Rumble in CBA Research Report 33 (1980). The year is c. 1020-1025

history.text: King Edward's charters named the minster at Wic, the wic-hythe and a haw in Hamtun.
history.source: Sawyer 1012 and 1008: https://esawyer.lib.cam.ac.uk/charter/1012.html

history.text: King Edward had seventy-six men (or seventy-nine) in the town. Twenty years on, sixty-five Frenchmen and thirty-one Englishmen had been settled beside them.
history.source: Domesday Book: https://opendomesday.org/place/SU4111/southampton/ ; Victoria County History, Hampshire 3 (1908)

eras.text: King Beorhtric's town, and King Offa's coin. The two great kings have shut their shores to each other's merchants; whether the order binds here nobody has said aloud (?), and the reeve has not asked. English cloth goes over to the Franks as pilgrims' bundles. Two thousand people, perhaps three: smiths, weavers, comb-makers, no farmers.

The ports are open again. Under King Ecgberht (from 802) the town is at its fullest: pennies with a West Saxon king's name are struck here or at Winchester, the pits behind the houses fill with Frankish pots, and wool men cross to the fair of Saint-Denis every October.

The fleets have found the water. Thirty-three crews are beaten on the shore in 840 and the ealdorman dies of it; two years on the place is plundered, or people say it was. Houses stand empty between lived-in ones. Nobody builds a wall. People with silver bury it.

A near-empty shore. St Mary's graveyard, the king's enclosure at the north end and a few fishers' houses remain; the streets go to grass. Hamtun is still the king's vill and the head of the shire, and its men fight for Winchester in 860. A ship that calls is noticed.

A new town with a ditch and a bank stands on the Test shore, a short walk south-west of the old hythe, and takes its trade. From about 928 two moneyers sit there by the king's law, and nothing above twenty pence may be bought outside a port. After 950 it thrives.

Plundered in 980, and most of its people killed or carried off. Rebuilt. In the winter of 994 Olaf's and Swein's fleet lies here, fed by all Wessex, waiting for sixteen thousand pounds: the worst guests and the best market the town has had. The pennies say HAMTUN or HAMWIC as the die-cutter pleases.

The great men swear to Cnut here in 1016, and there is one peace on both shores. The mint closes about 1023. The old town is 'Wic', a minster and a hythe named in King Edward's charters; the new one is Hamtun, with the king's seventy-six men, wine from Rouen, and French voices on the strand before 1066 is out.

sites.name: The wic-hythe
sites.see: A long shelving beach of gravel and grey mud on the Itchen, with a dozen clinker hulls drawn up stern to the water and props under their bilges. In front, porters wade with casks on their shoulders; behind, three gravel streets run straight up between thatched houses to the graveyard of St Mary's. No quay, no post, no tower. It smells of weed, tar and wet wool, and the light is flat and wide off the water.
sites.source: Morton 1992: boats drawn up on a shelving beach east of St Mary's; no quay or jetty known. The name wic-hythe is from Sawyer 1012 (1045). The toll is the table's 5%: no toll charter survives (?)

sites.name: The strand street
sites.see: A gravel street five paces wide along the top of the beach, the long sides of the houses facing it, each with an open shed where the goods lie: bolts of grey and brown cloth, black Frankish jugs in straw, a pair of grey quernstones against a doorpost. A weighing balance hangs in one doorway. Women spin as they walk. There is no market place; the street is the market.
sites.source: Morton 1992: a strand street along the shore; houses 10-12 m by 4-5 m with the long side to the street and an open shed; no market place found. Seine-valley black and grey wares are 18% of the pottery (Hodges 1981)

sites.name: The king's yard
sites.see: A fenced enclosure at the north end of the main street, where the gravel is widest. Inside, a long thatched house with a carved door-frame, a store on posts, two horses under a lean-to. A man with a rod stands in the gateway and people wait in the street to be called. Wood-smoke, horse, and roasting meat when the king is expected.
sites.source: Morton 1992: the site SOU 47 at the north end, with bronze spoons and a fork-spoon, guessed to be the king's enclosure and lived in into the tenth century (?). No hall has been found; Hamtun is 'the royal vill' in Sawyer 288 (840)

sites.name: The shore church
sites.see: A small timber church of two rooms a little above the tide line, thirteen paces long, with a tall wooden cross standing before its door and a crowded graveyard round it, the newest mounds still bare. Its one small window holds greenish glass that throws a spot of light on the altar cloth. Inside it smells of beeswax and damp thatch, and the sea can be heard through the wall.
sites.source: Morton 1992: the timber church of site SOU 13, 12.9 by 4.2 m, perhaps glazed, in a graveyard of about a hundred, perhaps with a standing cross before it. Leland saw a chapel of St Nicholas 'where the old parish church of Old Hampton stood'

sites.name: St Mary's above the hythe
sites.see: Where the three river streets meet the main street there is a wide fenced graveyard on the highest ground the town has, which is not high. A timber church stands in it among rows of grass mounds with wooden markers. From its gate the whole beach can be seen, every hull and who is loading her. Rooks, wind, and the bell for the hours, struck by hand.
sites.source: Morton 1992: St Mary's was probably the main graveyard from about 750; it is the 'mynster aet Wic' of 1045 (Sawyer 1012) and the mother church of Southampton since. Nothing early has been seen in the ground, so the timber church is a guess (?). The founding by Birinus in 634 is not claimed

sites.name: The comb-makers' sheds
sites.see: Three open sheds on the street down to the hythe. In the nearest a woman saws cattle bone into plates on a block that is the grey backbone of a whale, and the floor is white with offcuts. Next door a man pours bronze into a stone mould for pins, and a boy draws wire. Sawdust of bone, hot metal, a glue pot. Finished combs hang on a string like fish.
sites.source: Morton 1992; Ellis and Andrews 2006: by Chapel Road 1,668 bone offcuts, mostly cattle, and a whale's vertebra used as a chopping block; ingot moulds, crucibles and pin wire nearby. Workshops stood house by house, not by quarter

sites.name: The smiths at the north crossing
sites.see: Two smithies face each other where the cross street meets the main street, each an open-sided shed with a clay hearth and a leather bellows. A lump of raw iron bloom sits by the anvil like a burnt loaf. Sparks, the double ring of two hammers, slag crunching underfoot in the street. A row of clench nails cools on a plank for the boat menders.
sites.source: Morton 1992: two smithies at Six Dials and slag at six other spots; iron came in as bloom. Clench nails in the town: Addyman and Hill 1969

sites.name: Beorngyth's ale-house
sites.see: A long house one street back from the beach with its door open and a bush on a pole above it. Benches along both walls, a hearth in the middle, a pottery lamp on a post, and a Frankish black jug that is only brought out for those who pay first. On the lintel sits a smooth grey stone axe nobody can explain. Ale, peat-brown smoke, eel broth, four tongues at once.
sites.source: invented: no ale-house has been dug. The house is the town's common house (Morton 1992); lamps of pot and stone, and a Stone Age flint axe kept as a curio, are finds (Addyman and Hill 1969; Morton 1992)

sites.name: The wool houses
sites.see: A row of house-ends toward the hythe with plank doors and no windows. One stands open: sacks of wool to the rafters, a loom leaning in the door with its clay weights swinging, bolts of cloth laid on a trestle with the makers' knots in the selvedge. Two old casks from the Seine hold the well-lining nobody has got round to. Lanolin, dust, a dog asleep on the best cloth.
sites.source: Morton 1992; Bourdillon and Coy 1980: sheep were kept old for the fleece, loom weights, pin-beaters and wool combs in every house; wells lined with old casks. That wool and cloth were the export is likely, not proven

sites.name: The boat strand
sites.see: South of the houses the gravel gives way to salt marsh, a shingle spit and a small still lagoon. On the last firm ground a hull lies on her side with three strakes off, new oak pale against the old, and a pitch pot smokes over a fire of offcuts. Beyond her the wide grey water runs down toward Wight. Curlews, adzes, the smell of tar and hot moss.
sites.source: Morton 1992: salt marsh, a shingle spit and a small lagoon south of the town. No yard has been dug: the waterfront is unexcavated (?). Clinker ships and clench nails: Addyman and Hill 1969; oak felled near Hamwic in 769 for an English ship (Ufkes 2012)

sites.name: The old stone work across the river
sites.see: Upriver, in the bend of the Itchen on the far bank, grey walls of flint and red tile stand higher than a house, with elder growing from the top and no roof anywhere inside. A ferryman keeps a flat boat on the mud below them. It is the only stone in sight, and people cross themselves or do not, according to who built it in their grandmother's telling.
sites.source: Morton 1992: the Roman walls of Clausentum on the east bank, 1.4 km upstream. Perhaps the fort with 188 m of wall of the Burghal Hidage's 150 hides (?). The ferry is invented

sites.name: Hamtun on the Test shore: the moneyers' benches
sites.see: Inside the ditch and bank of the new town, by the gate on the landward side, two benches under one thatch. At each a man sets a blank on a die fixed in a block and strikes once. A reeve's man counts the pennies into a bag and a balance stands between them. Outside, a street of new houses runs down to a second beach on the wider river. Charcoal, hot silver, the stroke of the hammer.
sites.source: II Aethelstan (c. 928): two moneyers at Hamtun, and no buying above 20 pence outside a port. The ditched town on the Test shore from c. 900: Morton 1992. The mint closed c. 1020-1025 (Addyman and Hill 1968). ports_793.json gives Hamwic no mint: that is true of 793 and not of 928

people.name: Herewald
people.trait: King Beorhtric's reeve at the wic: witnesses sales, takes the king's share, and has made an art of not being told things officially.
people.want: A full beach, a quiet king, and nothing in writing that he would have to obey.
people.fear: To end like Beaduheard, the reeve at Dorchester, who rode down to three strange ships to bid them to the king's vill and was killed on the sand.
people.voice: Slow, friendly West Saxon. Says 'I have not heard that' when he has.
people.looks: About forty-five, broad and red-faced, brown beard going grey, a russet cloak with a round bronze brooch, a long knife at his belt, a peeled hazel rod of office in his hand.
knows: who is on the beach, whose ship she is and what she landed
the king's share and how to pay it without a quarrel
what is said at Winchester about King Offa, the king's father-in-law
which strangers he has let land this year, and which he sent on
Ine's law on traders: buy before witnesses, or be held a thief

ties.note: the Mercian wic-reeve at Lundenwic knows most of what goes round by Hamwic, and sends him courteous messages about it
takes the Frisian's gifts and does not ask what is in a pilgrim's bundle
the factor has paid for more feasts in the king's yard than the reeve likes to count
the pilot tells him what sails are in the water before they reach the beach
the priest says a bundle on a pilgrim's back is a lie told in church clothes
not he but his grandson, reeve in King Aethelwulf's sons' time, saw the Frankish prefect off across the sea in December (?)
witnesses the wool man's sales and eats at his table at Lammas; he calls it keeping an eye on the king's share
the king's share on her ale is two brewings behind, and he drinks the difference
not he but his heir: in the years of the fleets the king's yard feeds the ealdorman's men when the shire is called out
the reeves of this shore are one family, by their own telling, down to the port-reeve of Hamtun two hundred years on (?)

lines.greet: A Frisian. Good. Draw her up above the weed. I am Herewald, the king's reeve. You sell before witnesses here, and I am usually one of them.
lines.greet_again: Your boat I know by her patch. Same berth. The king's share is the same, and so am I.
rumour: A king's order about Frankish ships? I have not seen it. If I see it I must obey it, so I take care where I look.
Three ships came to Portland in the king's first years. The reeve there thought they were traders. Now I count the shields before I ride down.
Our lady the queen is King Offa's daughter. So we love the Mercians here. Write that down if anybody asks you.
The wic-reeve at Lundenwic sent to ask what passes through my beach. I answered that the tide does, twice.
lines.saying: Buy in front of two honest men. If you cannot find two, buy in front of me.
lines.to_heir: Your father paid the king's share without being asked twice. Draw her up where he did.
lines.farewell: Go with the long flood. And if anyone at Lundenwic asks, you were never here, and I was very civil.

people.source: invented: the dossier assumes a king's reeve and names none. Here- and -wald are English name parts. The office and its fear from Beaduheard at Portland, c. 789 (Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 787; Aethelweard). Witnessed buying: Ine 25. The id is the office: quentovic.json ties its prefect Grippo (855-870) to 'hamwic.reeve', meaning his heir

people.name: Hildulf
people.trait: Thiadbod's man on the West Saxon shore: a quiet Frisian who ropes English cloaks into square bundles and finds pilgrims to carry them over.
people.want: A share of his own instead of a wage, and a house here that is in his name and not his master's.
people.fear: Peace between the kings, which closes the gap he lives in; and Thiadbod finding out how the tally really stands.
people.voice: Dry, low, counts aloud in Frisian when he is thinking. Never names his master without calling him generous.
people.looks: About thirty-three, lean, sandy hair cut short, a grey Frisian cloak worn short to the knee, a split tally stick and a coil of cord at his belt, rope burns on both hands.
knows: what English cloth fetches on the Canche and the Seine this month
which pilgrims are pilgrims and which are being paid
every creek between here and Wight where a boat can lie unseen at low water
when Thiadbod's ship is due and what she carries
a few runes, the Frisian way, which he taught to the comb-maker

ties.note: runs his master's English cloth through the half-open wic and keeps the tally
the same master at home: Hildulf's passage, his cloak and his debts are all Thiadbod's
pays for the reeve's blindness in feasts and Frankish wine
showed her the runes one winter; she cut her name on a cow's toe bone to prove it
buys the cloth the Englishman wanted, with the Frisian's deeper purse
the toll clerk on the Canche opens bundles looking for his knots
the pilot showed him every creek below the town, for silver, and has been cooler since he saw what the creeks were wanted for
Hildgyth at Dofras knows his knots on other people's bundles, and says his pilgrims carry cloth that should have crossed in her name

lines.greet: From Dorestad? Then you know whose man I am. He is a generous man. Stand there and hold this cord while I knot it.
lines.greet_again: You again, and your small boat. Small is good. Nobody counts what comes out of a small boat.
rumour: A pilgrim owns nothing, so a toll man asks him nothing. It is a holy thing, poverty. I have six of it going over on Thursday.
The Franks want the cloaks longer. Our weavers want the same price for more cloth. Somebody will write a letter about it.
My master's news is always a week old when he gives it. Mine is from this morning. That is the difference in our wages.
lines.saying: A short cloak covers a long conscience.
lines.to_heir: I roped bundles with your father. He tied a better knot than he told a lie. Sit down.
lines.farewell: Low water shows every creek. Come back then, if you want to learn this shore.

people.source: invented in the chain black_stones (Design/content/chains/black_stones.md: 'Hildulf, Thiadbod's man at Hamwic', Hild- + -ulf). The half-open wic is the spine's invention: how far the ban of c. 789-796 reached is not recorded (?). One rune on the Hamwic bone looks Frisian (R. I. Page in Addyman and Hill 1969)

people.name: Leofstan
people.trait: A wool and cloth man of the strand street, shut out of the Frankish fairs for six years by two kings' quarrel and still angry about each one.
people.want: To stand at the fair of Saint-Denis in October with a full purse, and to bring home Seine wine in his own casks.
people.fear: That the Frisians will own the carrying of English wool before an Englishman owns a second ship.
people.voice: Loud, quick, counts in scores. Calls every bolt of cloth 'she'. Laughs before the joke is finished.
people.looks: About thirty-six, tall and big-handed, fair hair tied back, a good madder-red tunic under a brown cloak, a pair of small shears on a thong round his neck and wool grease to the elbows.
knows: the price of wool and cloth here, and what the same bolt fetches at Rouen
when the shearing is and which estates send the best fleece
the way up the Seine and what the monks of Saint-Denis ask for a cask
which Frankish ship-masters pay in good pennies
that there is another Leofstan, at Lundenwic, with a ship under seal on the Canche

ties.note: no kin: the Lundenwic skipper of the same name, whose wool rotted on the Canche; each is tired of being taken for the other
the Frisian factor outbids him for the best cloth with another man's silver
his wife's sister; he sells her combs over the sea and she says he keeps too much
the reeve witnesses his sales and eats at his table at Lammas
bought Mercian fleece on credit in a thin year and has paid half
lodges at her ale-house by the Seine every autumn and pays in good wool cloth
the cooper at Rouen, whom he pays on the day: a custom the cooper finds strange and fine
the abbot who keeps the Frankish tolls let his casks through once, and said so twice
Leofrun on the Strand says West Saxon cloth goes out through Hamwic at her price while her port is shut; he says she is welcome to move

lines.greet: Leofstan. Wool, mostly. Feel that: she is from ewes six winters old, and no Frisian has had his thumb on her yet.
lines.greet_again: The Dorestad boat. Come in out of the wind. I have a bolt put by that I would not show your friend with the tally stick.
rumour: The fair of Saint-Denis opens nine days into October. A day and a night to Rouen, then the river. I have missed six. I do not mean to miss a seventh.
There is a Leofstan at Lundenwic whose wool went sour under a Frankish seal. Not me. People pay me his sympathy and him my bills.
The king's sheep are kept till they are old, for the fleece. Then we eat them. That is why the wool is good and the dinner is not.
lines.saying: Wool on the sheep is the king's. Wool in the sack is mine. Wool on the sea is God's.
lines.to_heir: Your father and I bought cask for cask at the fair and argued over every one. I miss the arguing. Have you his temper?
lines.farewell: If you make the Seine before me, tell the cellarer at Saint-Denis an Englishman is coming with silver. He will not believe you.

people.source: invented in the chain wine_fleet (Design/content/chains/wine_fleet.md: 'Leofstan of Hamwic', Leof- + -stan; unlock_partner_leofstan). 'Saxon' traders at the October fair of Saint-Denis: the charters of 709 and 753 (Morton 1992). Old wool sheep: Bourdillon and Coy 1980. The namesake is quentovic.leofstan, another writer's man

people.name: Catte
people.trait: A comb-maker in bone and antler who can cut four runes and is prouder of that than of the combs.
people.want: Antler, which makes a better comb than cattle bone and does not come to this shore often enough.
people.fear: Her eyes going, and her name being forgotten: which is why she scratches it on things.
people.voice: Short sentences, eyes on the work. Teases without smiling. Asks what a thing is made of before she asks what it costs.
people.looks: About thirty, small and wiry, dark hair under a linen cap, a brown gown with sleeves tied back, bone dust to the wrists, a little saw in her hand and a comb scratched with a fish hung at her belt.
knows: what a dozen combs fetch here and what antler would fetch if you brought it
who in the town makes pins, whorls and wire, and who makes them badly
four runes, and what they spell
what the old people said lay under the mounds the houses were built over
what her sister's husband really gets for her combs over the sea

ties.note: the Frisian taught her the runes over one winter; one of hers is cut the Frisian way
her sister's husband, who carries her combs to Rouen
they trade riddles across the street, and the alewife usually wins
the priest threw old bones from the mounds out with the rubbish when the graveyard moved; some were her kin
the craftsman on Walichrum whose work comes over with the Frisian ships; she calls it showy and looks at it for a long time (?)
a comb-maker on the Strand who says a comb does not need to be read; she says his need to be counted, and he cannot

lines.greet: Mind the block. It is a whale's back. No, I did not catch it. What have you got that is antler?
lines.greet_again: The Frisian with the small boat. Did you bring antler? Then sit anyway. You can hold the plate while I saw.
rumour: I cut my name on a cow's toe. Four staves. The Frisian says one is wrong. I say it is mine and I may spell it how I like.
There were mounds where the houses by the cross street stand. Spears in them, the old people said. Now there is a cess pit. That is a town for you.
A man brought a shell-beast's bone from the far south, green as a pond. I offered to make it a comb. He would not sell.
lines.saying: A comb has many teeth and bites nobody. That is more than I can say for my sister's husband.
lines.to_heir: Your mother's comb was mine. The one with the fish. If she still has it, I made it well.
lines.farewell: Antler. Remember it. Red deer, not too old, and not cut by a fool.

people.source: invented person; the name is one reading of the runes 'catae' cut on a cow's toe bone from Hamwic ('cat', or someone called Cat(t) or Catte: R. I. Page in Addyman and Hill 1969). The whale-vertebra block, the fish-scratched comb, the green turtle bone and the mounds built over are finds (Morton 1992; Garner 1993; Ellis and Andrews 2006). That a woman made combs is our guess (?)

people.name: Ceolhelm
people.trait: The priest of the shore church, schooled at Nursling where Boniface taught: a careful man with a head full of Aldhelm's riddles and a parish full of sailors.
people.want: Glass for the east window, a book of his own, and pilgrims who are pilgrims.
people.fear: The two infants somebody put in a rubbish pit unbaptised; and what Bishop Cyneberht will say of his town when he hears.
people.voice: Gentle, exact, a schoolman's English with Latin tucked in. Sets a riddle the way other men offer ale.
people.looks: About forty-eight, thin and stooped, tonsured grey hair, a plain undyed gown and a dark cloak pinned with bone, ink on his right thumb, a wax tablet tied to his girdle.
knows: the feasts and fasts, and when the church will bury a stranger
which ship-masters take pilgrims for an honest fare, as Willibald's did
Aldhelm's riddles by heart, and Bede on the two tides that meet off the Hamble
what is in the book chest at Nursling and who may borrow
who in the town has not been to Mass since Easter

ties.note: he preaches against false pilgrims and the reeve stands at the back looking at the roof
she has not forgiven the bones from the old plots; he has not forgiven the runes
she sends him eels on fast days and the worst of the gossip on all days
his own bishop Cyneberht went to Rome with the archbishop about 801; Ceolhelm found the bishop's men a ship (?)
a Northumbrian who reads is rare on this beach; they talk about Bede until the tide is lost
the singing canon at Rouen, fond of riddles; they send each other one a year by the wool ships, and pilgrims with a tablet in their hands
the abbot who teaches at Dommoc has Aldhelm by heart too: each has heard that the other has a word wrong (?)
Eadhun of Christ Church trades him a leaf of Tatwine for a leaf of Aldhelm written fair, by any pilgrim going east

lines.greet: God keep you. You came in on the second high water, I think. Bede knew about that. Do sailors read Bede? No. Sit down.
lines.greet_again: The Frisian who listens. Good. I have a new one for you: I am a house that holds sunlight and drowns no one. A cask, of course.
rumour: Six pilgrims went over on Thursday, each with a square bundle. Saint Peter will be surprised how well dressed the English poor have become.
The old burying plots are built over now. I moved what I could to holy ground. Not everyone thanks me.
Bishop Cyneberht has not come down since Whitsun. When a bishop stays away it is either very good or very bad.
A ship-master took Willibald over from this water for a fare, seventy years back. They pitched tents at Rouen. The fare has gone up.
lines.saying: The sea gives a man time to think and nothing to write on.
lines.to_heir: I buried your father's steersman by the cross. Your father paid for the wax. I say his name at All Saints, and your father's.
lines.farewell: Go with God, and come to Mass before you load, not after. The wind does not mind which.

people.source: invented; Ceol- and -helm are English name parts. Nursling, six km off, was Boniface's school; Aldhelm (d. 709) was the West Saxons' riddler; Bede IV.16 on the tides off the Hamble; Cyneberht bishop of Winchester to 801/3, who went to Rome with Archbishop Aethelheard (Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 799). The infants in the pits and the moved graves: Morton 1992. Willibald's crossing: Huneberc

people.name: Eadhun
people.trait: A shore fisher who takes ships up and down the long water for a fee, and knows to the foot where the mud begins.
people.want: A boat big enough to go outside Wight; and a son who looks at the water instead of at Leofstan's daughter.
people.fear: Strange sails that come in without a hail. His elder brother rode down to Portland strand behind the reeve Beaduheard and did not ride back.
people.voice: Unhurried, sing-song shore English. Talks about the water as about a neighbour he gets on with.
people.looks: About forty, short and thick, skin like a boot, bleached hair, a patched tunic to the knee and bare legs grey with mud, an eel spear over his shoulder and a sounding pole taller than he is.
knows: the double tide: when she stands, when she runs, and how long a hull may sit on the flats
the shingle spit at the water's mouth and the two ways round Wight
what sails are in the water today, a tide before the reeve knows
where the eels, the bass and the oysters are, by the moon
what happened at Portland, as his brother's horse-boy told it

ties.note: is paid a penny a moon to watch the water's mouth and say what comes
has asked the widow twice; she says a man who smells of eels may ask a third time in a dry month
showed the Frisian the creeks, for silver, and wishes now that he had not
the Kentish pilots pass word along the coast of sails seen; it reaches him in four days (?)
not he but his sons, who watch the water's mouth for the ealdorman in the years of the fleets

lines.greet: You came up well. Most strangers wait for the ebb and get half of one. She floods twice here. Did nobody tell you?
lines.greet_again: I saw your sail at the spit and said to the reeve: the small Frisian. He said: good, he pays.
rumour: Thirteen sea miles from the spit to the hythe, soft mud both sides. You can sit a boat on it and take no hurt. Getting her off is another prayer.
My brother went down to Portland strand with the reeve to greet three ships. So now I look at how a ship sits before I wave.
Oysters are fat till the cuckoo comes. After that you eat them at your own risk and somebody else's ale.
lines.saying: The tide waits for no man, but here she comes back to see if you have changed your mind.
lines.to_heir: I took your father up this water in a fog with a pole and a prayer. You have his way of standing in a boat.
lines.farewell: Leave on the long stand, an hour after she tops. Keep the dead tree on the oak wood. You will carry water all the way down.

people.source: invented; Ead- and -hun are English name parts. The water from a seventeenth-century account quoted by Morton 1992: 13 km of 'good and even soundings', mud flats 'safe for any body to rest on'; the double high water; eel, flounder, bass and mullet, oysters and winkles (Bourdillon and Coy 1980). Beaduheard at Portland, c. 789. The brother is invented; the proverb is turned from a later one (?)

people.name: Beorngyth
people.trait: A widow who brews for the beach and hears everything twice: once from the man who did it and once from the man who saw.
people.want: Her benches full, her debts in, and the pilot to wash before he asks again.
people.fear: Fire in the thatch; and a night when all the benches are full of men who came in one ship and paid for nothing.
people.voice: Warm, sharp, never raises her voice. Gives a riddle with a double meaning and a perfectly straight face.
people.looks: About forty, sturdy, a clean linen head-cloth, a blue-grey gown with a string of glass beads between two bronze pins, keys at her belt, sleeves wet to the elbow.
knows: every rumour on the beach and roughly how old it is
which crews are short a man and which men are short a crew
who owes whom in the town, and who pays
riddles: the plain sort and the other sort
what the Frankish masters say about their own king when they have drunk

ties.note: she has refused him twice and kept his eel-traps mended all the same
feeds the priest on fast days and tells him what his flock would not
trades riddles and bone pins with the comb-maker across the street
the king's share on her ale is two brewings behind, and the reeve drinks the difference
an Englishwoman who keeps a bench for English crews on the Canche; they send each other men who can be trusted, and warnings about the rest
the ale-wife on the Strand tells the onion riddle too; each says she had it first, and both had it from a sailor (?)

lines.greet: Bench by the door for new faces, where I can see them. Ale is a penny for more than you can carry. The black jug is for wine, and for those who pay first.
lines.greet_again: Your bench is warm. A Frank sat on it all last week telling me what his king would do. Then his king did not.
rumour: A master in from Rouen says the Seine wine is good this year. He said it last year too, of worse wine.
Here is one. I stand tall in a bed, hairy below, and a pretty girl who grips me weeps for it. An onion. Shame on you.
The Frisian factor pays for everything and owns nothing. The reeve owns everything and pays for nothing. I serve both.
The stone on my lintel fell with the thunder, my husband said. It keeps the lightning off. So far the roof agrees.
lines.saying: Men are thirstiest the morning after mead.
lines.to_heir: Your father drank slowly and paid quickly. Sit where he sat. We shall see which half you got.
lines.farewell: Come back with news and I will stand you the first cup. Come back with old news and you stand mine.

people.source: invented; Beorn- and -gyth are English name parts. The onion riddle is paraphrased, not quoted, from Exeter Book 25 (texts_793.json exeter_25_onion). The saying is turned from the Durham Proverbs ('after mead men mostly thirst', our rendering (?)). The flint axe kept as a curio, glass beads and Frankish black jugs are finds (Morton 1992; Hodges 1981)

people.name: Wulfheard
people.trait: Ealdorman under King Ecgberht and King Aethelwulf: an old soldier who rode into Kent for his king in 825 and fights his last fight on this beach.
people.want: Warning. A day's notice of sails turns a slaughter of townsmen into a slaughter of raiders.
people.fear: That the shore has no wall and the king no ships; that he is too old to do this every summer.
people.voice: Few words, spoken as orders. Thanks a man once and remembers it for good.
people.looks: About sixty, tall and spare, white moustache, a mail shirt under a dark red cloak with a gilt brooch, a sword with a worn silver pommel, a helm carried by a boy behind him.
knows: how many men Hamtunscir can put on the beach in a day
where a fleet would land and where it could be caught on the mud at the ebb
what the king intends this summer, in part
which merchants brought true word of ships and which brought stories

ties.note: the reeve's heir keeps the king's yard and feeds his men when the shire is called out
the pilot's sons watch the water's mouth for him
her house on the Canche pays the same raiders two years on; a merchant who knows both shores carries the word (?)

lines.greet: You are the Frisian from the beach. What sails did you see between Wight and here? Count them for me. Slowly.
lines.greet_again: The merchant who can count. Good. Stand here. Tell me again what you saw off the Franks' shore.
rumour: Thirty-three crews is two thousand men, if they are full. I have the shire, and the mud. The mud is the better soldier.
The king gives land in this vill and trusts God for a wall. I trust God. I would like the wall as well.
I rode into Kent with the king's son in my youth and the Kentish king fled over the Thames. That was a war. This is weeding.
lines.saying: A man should not be too soon afraid, nor too soon glad.
lines.to_heir: Your house brought me word once, in time. I told the king whose word it was.
lines.farewell: If you see sails you cannot name, come back and say so. I pay better for that than the town pays for wine.

people.source: historical: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 823 (for 825: sent into Kent with Aethelwulf and Bishop Ealhstan) and 837 (for 840: 'Alderman Wulfherd fought at Hamton with thirty-three pirates', Ingram 1823 (wording not rechecked (?)), and died the same year). His age, looks and words are invented. The saying is Durham Proverbs, our rendering (?)

people.name: Aelfnoth
people.trait: The king's reeve of the port of Hamtun: carried off as a boy in the plundering of 980, bought back at Rouen for English pennies, and now the man who feeds the fleet that might have been the same one.
people.want: Every sale above twenty pence made inside the ditch before his witnesses; and one cup, taken from the minster at Wic, back on its altar.
people.fear: A second morning like the one when he was twelve. He counts the ships on the beach before he says his prayers.
people.voice: Even, careful, a little hoarse. Speaks Danish well enough to be cheated in it, and never says where he learned it.
people.looks: About thirty, lean, cropped brown hair, an old white scar round one wrist, a dark green cloak with a silver disc brooch, a ring of keys and a small balance in a leather case at his belt.
knows: the port's law: witnesses, the two moneyers, the toll on wine and on fish
how many crews lie on the beach and what Wessex sends to feed them
what a captive costs at Rouen, from the inside
which shipman of Rouen sells things that were not his to buy
who rode in to swear to Cnut, and who sent a cousin

ties.note: remembers a cargo of the Rouen shipman's that was not all wine: a cup he had last seen on the altar at Wic
stood at the gate in 1016 when the great men rode in to swear, and kept his office under the Dane
the tall Dane's quartermasters bought on his beach and paid in pennies struck at his own benches
the reeves of this shore have been one family since King Beorhtric, by their own telling (?)
the tollman at Billingsgate counted the fleet from the wall that he then had to feed; they compare sums

lines.greet: You buy and sell inside the ditch, before two of my witnesses. Above twenty pence, that is the king's law. Below it, that is my advice.
lines.greet_again: The house from over the sea. Your berth is where you left it. I have counted the beach this morning: you make it sixty-one.
rumour: I was sold on the bank at Rouen for nine shillings. An aunt paid. I know to the penny what I am worth, which is more than most men do.
Ninety-four crews, and all Wessex feeding them. They pay for ale in our own pennies. I have stopped being surprised.
A shipman of Rouen sold a cup at London that I knew. Wine on top of his cargo and other men's churches under it.
The die says HAMTUN one year and HAMWIC the next. The cutter cannot decide where we live. Nor can I.
lines.saying: A wall is a prayer made of turf. Say it every spring or it stops being heard.
lines.to_heir: Your father's house gave toward the price when the fleet lay here. It is written in my tally. Take the berth by the gate.
lines.farewell: If you put in at Rouen, look at what the shipmen sell beside their wine. Tell me what you see. I will know it.

people.source: invented, to stand for the unnamed reeve of the port (another writer's rotomagus.thorold is tied to 'hamwic.portreeve'). Aelf- and -noth are English name parts. The plundering of 980, the wintering of 994-995, the oath to Cnut in 1016, the pennies signed HAMTUN and HAMWIC, and II Aethelstan on witnessed buying are real (see history). Slaves sold at Rouen in his day: Warner of Rouen's Moriuht (LATER retellings). His price is invented

stories.title: The back door
stories.summary: While King Charles and King Offa have shut their shores to each other, the West Saxon wic stays half open, because its king is Offa's son-in-law and its reeve has taken care not to see an order. Thiadbod's factor sends English cloaks over the sea on pilgrims' backs, and a Frisian with a small boat is asked to choose between a third of the profit and a clean name on both shores.
stories.picture: The hythe at low sun: a lean Frisian in a short grey cloak ropes a square bundle onto the back of a stooping pilgrim, the reeve standing a little way off studying the sky, a small boat with a patched side on the gravel behind.

beats.text: The wic-reeve Wighelm turns Frankish hulls away and asks a Frisian twice whose man he is. A skipper on the foreshore says there is another beach, further west, where another king's reeve asks less.
Beorngyth says the ports are shut and the benches are full, both at once. She points with her chin at the Frisian by the door who pays for everything.
Hildulf is roping six square bundles for six pilgrims. He needs a boat nobody counts. A third of what the cloaks fetch on the Canche is yours if they pass; if they do not, he never met you.
Ceolhelm blesses pilgrims for the road to Rome and counts the bundles as he does it. He asks whether you carry men to God or cloth to market, and says he will pray for you either way.
At the toll house on the Canche the clerk Hildric knows Hildulf's knots. Pilgrims pass free. Whether these pass depends on the hour, the clerk's temper and how the bundles sit.
Hildgyth at Dofras can tell West Saxon cloth from Kentish by the selvedge. She says half the bundles going over the strait this year were roped by one Frisian's hand, and that she knows the knot.

There is a second back door, on the Orwell, where a reeve counts aloud and looks at the river. Thiadbod would give a share to know which river. Hildulf already has an idea, and is not telling his master.

Herewald feasts the Frisians who feed his beach. He will say, if you ask him well, how wide the gap is: as wide as a queen who is Offa's daughter and a king who would rather not write to his father-in-law.

Offa is dead three days before Lammas. If the kings' letter was written, the gap is closed and Hildulf splits a tally over his knee. If it was not, Thiadbod lays silver on a cask head and half is in your name.

endings.how: You carried the bundles while the ban stood, and took your share when it ended.
endings.text: The shut years paid better than the open ones will. Hildulf walks you down the shore at low water and names every creek, and an abbot on the Canche remembers your boat.
endings.reward: 600 to 1,300 d from the chain; unlock_pilot_solent or unlock_factor_hamwic; Hildulf a fast friend; the toll clerks of the Canche wary.

endings.how: You sold in the open street under the reeve's eye, paid the king's share and left the bundles on the beach.
endings.text: You made less, and everybody saw you make it. Herewald puts his rod across your berth so no one else takes it, and the priest says your name on a Sunday.
endings.reward: Herewald's witness (hamwic.unlock.reeves_witness); Ceolhelm a friend; first cargo rights when the ports open: quernstones sell dear here for a year.

endings.how: You ran the bundles, and when the peace came you paid the tolls you had slipped.
endings.text: It costs most of what you made. The clerk on the Canche writes it down twice to be sure he is not dreaming. Hildulf thinks you mad, and asks to work for you.
endings.reward: Half toll at Hamwic for 120 days (the chain's _paid_tolls); unlock_factor_hamwic with Hildulf as the man; standing with the church on both shores.

stories.reward: A man of your own on the West Saxon beach, or the knowledge of every creek below it, or a name the reeve will swear to.

stories.title: The cask, the cup and the shell
stories.summary: The priest of the shore church gives Aldhelm's riddles in Latin to anyone who will sit; the alewife and the comb-maker give the English kind, with two meanings. Each holds one part of a three-part riddle whose answer is something on this beach, and the comb-maker will teach four runes to whoever solves it.
stories.picture: The inside of the ale-house by lamplight: a thin priest with a wax tablet, a sturdy woman with a jug and a small woman holding up a cow's toe bone scratched with four runes, all three looking at the viewer and waiting.

beats.text: Ceolhelm sets Aldhelm's riddle of the wine cask, and then the glass cup. He will give them written on a tablet to a crew that has a reader, and says the third part is not in any book of his.

Beorngyth gives the oyster: a thing with no feet that the sea fed, opened with a knife and eaten raw. She says the priest's two and hers are all things that hold something, and the last one holds a name.

Catte shows a cow's toe bone with four runes. If you have the cask, the cup and the shell, she asks what holds a name. The answer is in her hand. She teaches the four staves, and which one the Frisian says is wrong.
Ravn turns the bone over and says the third stave is cut the Frisian way, not the northern. He gives a riddle of his own in return, and wants to know who on that beach had a Frisian for a teacher.
At Bede's house a monk knows Aldhelm's hundred and copies out the two you carry, corrected. He sends a third to the priest of the shore church, who has been wrong about one word for thirty years.
Tidburh at the Sarre crossing has an oyster bed of her own and the oyster's riddle with it, in a longer telling. She says the Hamwic woman had hers from a Kentish skipper and left out the best line.
Abbot Lull at Dommoc has Aldhelm's hundred by heart and knows who taught them to whom. Told how the priest at Hamwic says the cask, he corrects one word and is pleased for a week.
Eadhun the scribe will trade a leaf of Tatwine for a leaf of Aldhelm written fair, and asks who on the West Saxon shore still has Aldhelm whole.

endings.how: You answered all three and named what holds a name.
endings.text: Catte cuts your house's name on a bone plate, four staves and a fish, and rivets it into a comb. The priest pretends not to mind that the best riddle in his parish is in runes.
endings.reward: The texts aldhelm_78_cupa_vinaria, aldhelm_80_calix_vitreus and exeter_77_oyster for the chest; a first lesson in runes (learn runes); Catte's mark (hamwic.unlock.cattes_mark).

endings.how: You could not answer, but carried the riddles to a house of books and brought the correction back.
endings.text: Ceolhelm reads the corrected line twice, laughs at himself, and gives you the run of the tablet chest. Catte says a man who fetches is nearly as good as a man who thinks.
endings.reward: The same texts; Ceolhelm a fast friend; act read_text and copy_text free at the shore church; the thread's flag bk_carried.

endings.how: You gave up and paid the forfeit.
endings.text: A round for the house, and Beorngyth tells the answer to the whole bench before you have sat down. It is repeated to you at this beach for years.
endings.reward: Nothing but a bench where everybody knows you; morale for the crew, who enjoyed it.

stories.reward: Three riddle texts, four runes, and a comb with your name on it that people on other shores recognise.

stories.title: Thirty-three crews
stories.summary: The fleets that burn Dorestad from 834 find this water too. In 840 Ealdorman Wulfheard meets thirty-three ship-crews on the open beach and wins, and dies within the year; two years later the town is plundered, or so the Franks write. What a merchant saw at sea, and whom he told, decides how the day goes for those who know him here.
stories.picture: A grey dawn on the mud flats at half ebb: long ships stranded and leaning, men wading, a line of English shields along the gravel at the top of the beach and an old man in a red cloak on a horse behind them.

beats.text: Dorestad is burnt, and burnt again. Skippers who run west say the same fleets look into every river mouth on the way home, and that the West Saxon wic has no wall and no ships.
Wulfheard asks every master what sails he saw between Wight and the Franks' shore. He wants a day's warning. He says the mud will do the rest, if the shire is on the beach when the ebb starts.
Townspeople carry what they can over the ferry to the old stone work, and bury the rest behind their houses. A widow asks you to remember where, in case her sons do not come back to dig.
This year Ealdorman Wulfheard fought at Hamtun with thirty-three ship-crews and had the victory. If you brought word in time, the beach was manned at the ebb. He dies before the year is out.
A fleet falls on the Canche at first light, spares the houses that pay, and crosses the sea. The Franks write that it plundered Hamwic. Nobody on the English side writes anything.
This year there was great slaughter at London. Ceolmund counts the hulls on the Strand each morning, and asks every master up from the south whether Hamtun still stands.
Grass in the streets. From St Mary's gate you can count the roofs still thatched. The priest keeps a list of who went to Winchester, who went to the new ground, and who is under the mounds.
The widow's sons come back from Winchester with a spade, and ask along the shore for the Frisian who was told where.
The fleets that tried this water winter on Thanet now. At the toll post on the Wantsum Ealdorman Ealhhere asks what Wulfheard asked on the Itchen: how many keels, and where.

endings.how: You saw the fleet at sea and brought word to the ealdorman before it came.
endings.text: The shire stood on the gravel at the ebb, and the mud held thirty-three keels. Wulfheard told the king whose word it was. He died that winter; the king did not forget.
endings.reward: The thread's flag df_warned; the king's thanks: a toll-free beach here for your house (unlock_charter_hamwic); great standing with the West Saxons.

endings.how: You brought no warning, but you remembered where the widow's silver lay and saw it dug up for her sons.
endings.text: The sons come back from Winchester with a spade and your word for where. They build on the new ground on the Test shore, and their door is yours.
endings.reward: A fast friend's house at Hamtun from 900 for your heirs (hamwic.unlock.hamtun_door); a tenth of the hoard pressed on you, about 60 d.

endings.how: You kept clear of every open beach in those years.
endings.text: You lost nothing. When you come back the benches are gone and nobody on the shore knows your boat. The pilot's grandson asks what a Frisian wants here.
endings.reward: Your ship and cargo; every tie at Hamwic begins again from cool.

stories.reward: A king's memory of your house, or a family on the new ground that owes you its start.

stories.title: The fleet that wintered
stories.summary: In 980 the new town is plundered and most of its people killed or taken. Fourteen years later Olaf and Swein, beaten off from London, lie here all winter with ninety-four ships' crews, fed by Wessex and waiting for sixteen thousand pounds. A merchant can sell to the fleet, help the town pay its share, or stand in the church at Andover when a Northman king is confirmed.
stories.picture: A winter beach on the Test shore crowded with long ships under tilts of sailcloth, smoke from a hundred fires, a bishop on a mule and an ealdorman on a horse riding down through them toward one tall man who waits with his hands empty.

beats.text: This year the town was plundered by a ship-army, and most of the townsmen killed or taken. The moneyers' benches are overturned. A woman asks if you sail to Rouen, where captives are sold, and what one costs to buy back.
On the bank at Rouen English captives are sold from the Northmen's ships. Two speak the shore speech of Hamtun. The price is asked in pennies, and they are English pennies.
Three years before it lay at Hamtun the same fleet plundered Gipeswic. The moneyer there struck his town's part of the first tribute; the reeve of Hamtun will feed the men it was paid to.
On the Nativity of Saint Mary ninety-four ships come up to London and are beaten off. The tollman counts them from the wall and sends the number west before they have turned.

Ninety-four crews lie on the beach and all Wessex feeds them. They have silver coming and nothing to do till spring. Everything sells: ale, cloth, combs, news. The townsmen ask what you will give toward their share of the price.
Bishop Aelfheah lodges at the minster on his way to fetch Olaf to the king at Andover. He wants a man the Northmen will talk to, to carry word down to the ships that hostages are aboard.
Olaf has been confirmed with the king as his sponsor and has sworn never to come back in enmity. His ships go north with the first fair wind. Swein's do not swear anything.

The bishops, abbots and ealdormen ride in to Cnut at Hamtun, forswear the old king's sons and swear to the Dane. London has chosen Edmund. Whose pilot you are this summer will be remembered by the winner.

endings.how: You gave toward the town's share of the sixteen thousand pounds.
endings.text: The reeve writes your house among the townsmen who paid. It buys nothing that winter. Twenty years on, under Cnut, it is the reason your heir has a haw inside the ditch.
endings.reward: The thread's flag en_paid_share; a plot in Hamtun (unlock_plot_hamwic); the townsmen friendly for a generation.

endings.how: You sold to the fleet all winter.
endings.text: The best market of your life, paid in new pennies that had been other men's a month before. The crews go home rich and tell Ripa and Sliesthorp your name. The townsmen remember it too.
endings.reward: The thread's flag en_followed_silver; prices near double on ale, cloth and combs for one winter; friends in the Danish ports; Hamtun cool for years.

endings.how: You carried the bishop's word to the ships, and bought back the two from Rouen.
endings.text: Aelfheah remembers who went down among the tilts for him. When he is archbishop, and when he is killed at Greenwich, your house is named in the minster at Wic among those he prayed for.
endings.reward: Great standing with the English church; free lodging at the minster at Wic for your house; under Cnut, the king's writ comes easier (toward en_cnut_peace).

stories.reward: A place inside the ditch at Hamtun, or the fleet's silver and its friendship, or a bishop's prayers that outlast him.

stories.title: Wool over, wine back
stories.summary: Leofstan wants a partner with a hull for the run he was shut out of for six years: wool and cloth to Rouen after the June shearing, up the Seine to the fair of Saint-Denis in October, and wine home in casks that end their days lining Hamwic's wells. He is honest, loud and short of a second ship.
stories.picture: The wool houses on the strand street with a door open on sacks to the rafters; a tall fair man in a red tunic holds a bolt of cloth out at arm's length to a Frisian, a cask with a Seine cooper's mark standing between them as a table.

beats.text: Cynred the wool man on the Strand sold Leofstan Mercian fleece on the tally in a thin year and has been paid half. He will put by a bale for whoever carries the stick to Hamwic and brings back silver, or a good reason.

beats.when: year >= 796 and year < 821 and month >= 6 and month <= 8
beats.text: The shearing is in. Leofstan has more wool than his one ship carries and offers you the overflow at the shed price, 6 d the sack, if you will land it at Rouen and wait for him there.
A day and a night with the wind on the beam. On the bank at Rouen the cloth men want the cloaks long and the price short. Leofstan argues with all of them at once and enjoys it.
The fair of Saint-Denis, nine days into October, among the vineyards. Leofstan buys cask for cask beside you and says the monks have charters older than his grandfather naming Saxon traders here.
Home before Martinmas with the wine sound. Leofstan broaches one cask for the street and sells the rest to the king's yard and the church. The empty casks go down a well.

endings.how: You made the run with him and shared out fairly at the end.
endings.text: He swears partnership on the shore church's altar, with the reeve and the priest for witnesses, and his second ship is yours to send. His daughter keeps the tally and is better at it than either of you.
endings.reward: unlock_partner_leofstan: a sworn partner who sails a second hull between Hamwic and the Seine; first pick of the June wool (hamwic.unlock.first_fleece).

endings.how: You carried his wool and sold your own wine without him.
endings.text: No quarrel, exactly. He pays the freight to the penny and buys his own casks next year. You have the Seine trade in your head and no friend at either end of it.
endings.reward: About 200 d on the season and the knowledge of the Seine prices; Leofstan easy, no more.

endings.how: The wine did not keep, or you sold his wool short.
endings.text: He says nothing in the street and everything in the ale-house. For two summers the wool houses are shut to you until the shed price has gone up by a penny.
endings.reward: Whatever you kept; Leofstan wary, and the strand street with him.

stories.reward: A sworn English partner with a ship, and the wool-and-wine round between the Itchen and the Seine.

works.name: A well lined with casks
works.what: A well dug six paces deep behind the strand street and lined with two old Seine wine casks, one set on the other, for the use of the row and of your crew.
works.needs: A friend on the strand street to give the ground; two empty casks
works.gives: Fresh water at your berth: provisioning here costs less and takes no time; the row's goodwill.
works.picture: Two men lowering a stave-built cask on ropes into a square pit between house-ends, a third below in the dark, wet gravel heaped beside.
works.source: Morton 1992; Addyman and Hill 1969: wells up to 6 m deep, three lined with old casks; 21 wells at Six Dials alone

works.name: A gravel hard on the hythe
works.what: A strip of rammed gravel laid from the strand street down across the mud to the low-water line, as the streets are laid, so a hull can be loaded dry-shod at any state of the tide.
works.needs: The reeve's leave, and porters hired for a month
works.gives: Loading and unloading here take half the time; your berth is kept for you. The reeve takes it for the king's and thanks you.
works.picture: A pale gravel causeway running straight down a grey mud beach into the water, a small ship beached beside it and porters walking a cask down dry-shod.
works.source: The town's streets were of gravel, re-metalled up to five times (Morton 1992). No hard or jetty has been found: the waterfront is undug, so this is the player's own work (?)

works.name: A wool house of your own
works.what: A house plot on the strand street with a post-built house of the town's kind, ten paces by four, its long side to the street and an open shed for showing goods.
works.needs: Leofstan or the reeve to stand witness to the buying; a year's good standing in the town
works.gives: A store and a lodging here (unlock_plot_hamwic); goods can lie over a season and be sold when the Frankish ships come.
works.picture: A new thatched house with pale unweathered posts in a row of grey ones, its shed front open on stacked wool sacks, a Frisian hull drawn up below it.
works.source: Morton 1992: houses 10-12 m by 4-5 m, earth-fast posts, wattle and daub, thatch, an open shed. A 'haw' in Hamtun is named in Sawyer 1008 (1045)

works.name: Glass for the shore church
works.what: A window of Frankish glass for the east end of the timber church by the beach, and wax for a year, given in your house's name.
works.needs: A crate of glass landed here from the Rhine or the Seine; the priest's goodwill
works.gives: Your house is named at Mass; burial here for your dead; the priest's word for you along the coast.
works.picture: The east wall of a small timber church from inside, a priest on a ladder setting a pane of green glass into a wooden frame, coloured light on his sleeve.
works.source: Morton 1992: the church of site SOU 13 was perhaps glazed; over 200 finds of vessel glass in the town (Addyman and Hill 1969)

works.name: A share of the burh's bank
works.what: The keep of four poles of the bank and ditch of the new town on the Test shore: timber, turf and sixteen men's work each spring, as the king's reckoning asks of every hide.
works.needs: A house or a friend inside the ditch
works.gives: The standing of a townsman of Hamtun: you buy and sell above twenty pence here before the port's witnesses, and your goods are behind the bank when a fleet comes.
works.picture: Men with spades and baskets heaping a turf bank behind a line of oak posts, a wet ditch in front, new thatched roofs and a second beach behind.
works.source: The Burghal Hidage: 150 hides for Hamtun, one man from each hide, four men to each pole of wall (en.wikipedia Burghal Hidage). The ditched town from c. 900: Morton 1992. II Aethelstan on buying in a port

ships.note: The shore fishers' boats for eel, flounder, bass and oysters lie all along the mud; one can be had off the beach for ready silver, for lightering or for the creeks.
ships.picture: A small tarred clinker boat lying on grey mud beside an eel trap, a sounding pole laid across her thwarts.
ships.source: Bourdillon and Coy 1980 (the shore fishery); Morton 1992: rowed in shoal water, beached

ships.how: built to order over a winter
ships.note: Oak from the woods behind the water and clench nails from the smiths at the north crossing: a beach-landing sailing and rowing ship of the kind that took Willibald over. An oak felled here in 769 went into such a hull.
ships.picture: A half-planked clinker hull on the shingle by the salt marsh, pale new strakes, a pitch pot smoking, the wide water behind.
ships.source: Ufkes 2012 (oak felled 769 near Hamwic in an English clinker ship); clench nails in the town (Addyman and Hill 1969); Huneberc on Willibald's ship. No yard has been dug (?)

ships.note: Frankish and Frisian sea-going hulls beach here in the wool season; an old one changes hands now and then when her master would rather go home with silver. None is built here.
ships.picture: A deep-bellied merchant ship drawn up among smaller English boats, a Frankish master counting pennies on her rail.
ships.source: Hodges 1981 (the Seine trade); Morton 1992. That hulls were sold here is our guess (?)

ships.note: At the new town on the Test shore a townsman's ship can be hired with her master for the Rouen run, when the wine comes over.
ships.picture: A beached coaster on the Test shore below a turf bank, her master leaning on the stem with his arms folded.
ships.source: IV Aethelred: the men of Rouen with wine at London c. 1000; Morton 1992 on the tenth-century town. The hiring is our guess (?)

sayings.text: The tide waits for no man, but here she comes back to see if you have changed your mind.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner, on the double high water of this water (Morton 1992); the first half is a later proverb (?)

sayings.text: I have not seen the order. If I see it I must obey it, so I take care where I look.
sayings.source: invented: the reeve, on the ban of c. 789-796, whose reach is not recorded (?)

sayings.text: A short cloak covers a long conscience.
sayings.source: invented, turned from Notker's tale of Charles mocking the Frisians' short cloaks (Notker I.34, Grant 1907) and the king's letter of 796 asking that cloaks be as long as they used to be

sayings.text: A man should not be too soon afraid, nor too soon glad.
sayings.source: Durham Proverbs, our rendering (the number not checked (?))

sayings.text: Dear is the welcome one to the Frisian wife, when the ship stands in.
sayings.source: Exeter Book, Maxims I, lines 94-95, our rendering; said here of every Frisian who stays too long on the beach

sayings.text: Wool on the sheep is the king's. Wool in the sack is mine. Wool on the sea is God's.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner: the town was fed, probably from the king's estates, on old wool sheep (Bourdillon and Coy 1980)

sayings.text: What has no feet and was fed by the sea, and is opened with a knife and eaten raw by men who then ask for ale? Say it, and do not say my husband.
sayings.source: paraphrased, with the alewife's own ending, from Exeter Book riddle 77, the oyster (texts_793.json exeter_77_oyster; Tupper 1910 for the text)

sayings.text: This year the wool was good, and the Franks came for it, and nobody wrote anything down.
sayings.source: invented, in the Chronicle's manner: Hamwic has no annal of its own between 764 and 840

easter_eggs.text: On a shelf in the comb-makers' shed lies a cow's toe bone cut with four runes. They spell her name, or they spell 'cat'. One stave is cut the Frisian way.
easter_eggs.source: The Hamwic rune bone, read 'catae' by R. I. Page (Addyman and Hill 1969)

easter_eggs.text: A Frankish master shows a flat bone, green and heavy, from a shelled sea-beast of the far south. Nobody on the beach has a word for the animal.
easter_eggs.source: A green turtle's bone from African waters, found at Hamwic (Morton 1992)

easter_eggs.text: A well-digger brings up the shoulder blade of a small long-eared beast nobody can name. A Frank says they eat them at home, and that they live in holes.
easter_eggs.source: A rabbit's shoulder blade in a Hamwic well, when England bred no rabbits (Morton 1992)

easter_eggs.text: At the reeve's table lies a little bronze spoon with two prongs at the other end. He uses it for oysters and says it came from the king's own board.
easter_eggs.source: A bronze fork and spoon in one from site SOU 47 (Morton 1992). An odd thing in its day, not a table fork

easter_eggs.text: A little wooden box under the comb-maker's bench holds eleven small thick silver coins of the old kind, bright as the day they were struck. Her grandmother's. She will not sell them and cannot spend them.
easter_eggs.source: Eleven sceattas found 'in a little box', as new (Addyman and Hill 1968). The town struck its own sceattas from the 720s

easter_eggs.text: The planks of a ship built here in your grandfather's day, of oak felled the year after King Pippin died, lie in a bank on the island of Walichrum. A Frisian there will tell you so without being asked.
easter_eggs.source: Ufkes 2012; places/walichrum.json tells the other end of it

easter_eggs.text: The grass mounds left standing between the houses by the cross street have no crosses on them. Children are told not to play there, and do.
easter_eggs.source: Cook Street (SOU 254): nine graves, three ring-ditches, mounds left standing (Garner 1993)

easter_eggs.text: The eel broth has small bones in it and people chew them. Ask for bread with it.
easter_eggs.source: Eel bones crushed by human teeth, from a Hamwic cess pit (Ellis and Andrews 2006)

easter_eggs.text: In King Cnut's years a child on the Test shore sets a stool at the tide line and tells the sea to stop. Her mother fetches her in wet. Nobody thinks it worth telling.
easter_eggs.source: invented: Henry of Huntingdon's tale of Cnut and the tide (12th century, LATER) names no place, and Southampton's claim to it is modern

unlocks.how: Sell openly and pay the king's share at three calls running, or end the back door story with an open hand.
unlocks.gives: Herewald, and his heir after him, swears to your sales: no lawsuit over a purchase here can go against you, and your berth on the hythe is kept.

unlocks.what: The knowledge of the long water and the double tide
unlocks.how: Hire Eadhun three times, or walk the shore at low water with Hildulf at the end of the chain black_stones.
unlocks.gives: unlock_pilot_solent: no pilot's fee here, no waiting for the tide at this port, and the creeks below the town to lie in unseen.

unlocks.what: A man of your own at the hythe
unlocks.how: Finish the chain black_stones at Hamwic with a share, or take on Hildulf after paying the slipped tolls.
unlocks.gives: unlock_factor_hamwic: goods left here are sold for you at the season's best price, less his tenth.

unlocks.what: First pick of the June wool
unlocks.how: Swear partnership with Leofstan (unlock_partner_leofstan), or keep a wool house on the strand street for two shearings.
unlocks.gives: Wool and cloth at the shed price, about a quarter under the street, from the shearing to Lammas each year.

unlocks.what: A comb with your house's name in runes
unlocks.how: Answer the three riddles of the cask, the cup and the shell; or bring Catte antler three times.
unlocks.gives: A first lesson in runes (learn runes); combs from her bench at cost; an heirloom the house keeps (unlock_heirloom_cattes_comb) that her kin on other beaches recognise.

unlocks.what: Your house named at the shore church
unlocks.how: Pay for the glass (hamwic.work.glass), or bury a crewman here and pay for the wax.
unlocks.gives: Burial and sanctuary here without a fee; the priest's tablet of introduction to Nursling and to the monks on the Seine.

unlocks.what: A door on the new ground
unlocks.how: Keep trust with the townspeople in the raid years (the story Thirty-three crews), or pay toward the town's share in 994.
unlocks.gives: From 900, lodging and a store with a townsman's family inside the ditch at Hamtun, for your heirs (toward unlock_plot_hamwic).
